newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Company chiefs said likely to be first-borns.
newsitem.headline: Company chiefs said likely to be first-borns.

text.p: Top business executives, like dictators and supporters of capital punishment, are more than likely to be the first-born in their families, a U.S. researcher said on Thursday.

But when decisions on radical changes in company operations are taken, chances are high that they originate with junior board members who have at least one older sibling, he told the Davos World Economic Forum.

The twin messages were brought to the Forum, an annual gathering of global chief executives as well as political financial decision-makers, by Frank J. Sulloway of the Massachusetts Institute of Technology.

"Tough-mindedness, which brings many business people to the top, is a first-born trait, and there is no doubt that chief executives tend to be the elder child in a family," he told an opening session at the week-long event.
But Sulloway, who has spent 25 years studying the effect of family birth order on personality, said the traits that brought a manager to the top did not always help when companies were facing crises.

"The later-borns, especially third or fourth children, are more open to new ideas and new ways of doing things and are more likely to come up with revolutionary solutions when they are needed," he told Reuters in a later interview.

Sulloway's conclusions are based on wide research in archives in Europe and the United States on the family background of political leaders, scientists and thinkers from the Middle Ages to modern times.

Drawing on a vast database that he has accumulated during the project, he concluded that first-borns tend to identify with their parents and support the social and political status quo as well as hard-line, authoritarian means to maintain it.
Later-borns, although very open to change, are also more sensitive to the views, and sufferings, of others.
In the French Revolution, says Sulloway who recently published a book "Born to Rebel" on his findings, first-borns among the leaders of the new order backed the Terror to maintain it.

But during the Protestant Reformation movement 300 years earlier, later-borns were more likely to adopt the new faith and to suffer for it, being 46 times more likely to suffer martyrdom for "apostasy" than first children.

Right-wing revolutionaries, like Germany's Adolf Hitler who was the first surviving child in his family, are 18 times less likely to be later-borns than left-wing revolutionaries, like Russia's Vladimir Lenin, Sulloway says.

In science, his findings show, radical departures originated with later children like Charles Darwin whose Theory of Evolution attacked the predominant religious views of his age, and astronomer Nicholas Copernicus who broke with the official teaching of his time and insisted that the Earth revolved around the Sun, and not the reverse.
"A lot of research work has still to be done on our modern business culture but it is clear the results hold there too," says Sulloway. "And it emerges in many different ways."

One major U.S.-based investment fund, he says, is run in an autocratic manner by a first child, and demands a heavy front-end payment from new investors. Another, run as a collective, is more open to new trends and much less demanding.
"A survey of company boards' behaviour would find a significant difference on how first- and later-borns vote on high-risk and radical decisions," Sulloway told Reuters.
